competitions.name: AssetOpsBench
competitions.tagline: Benchmark LLM agents on multi-step industrial asset operations and maintenance tasks over MCP tools.
competitions.description: AssetOpsBench provides 141+ reproducible industrial scenarios spanning IoT, failure-mode, work-order, vibration and time-series-model domains, exposed to agents through six MCP servers. Agents are scored offline by an LLM judge (Llama-4-Maverick-17B) against a six-dimensional rubric covering reasoning, execution, tool use and data handling, plus newer static-JSON scorers. It is run by IBM Research and has powered public competitions (CODS 2025, IJCAI 2026) with 500+ submissions, and is accepted at KDD 2026.

participation.howToSubmit: Run an agent (plan-execute, claude-agent, openai-agent, deep-agent, opencode-agent, stirrup-agent or direct-llm-agent) against a scenario suite, save trajectories and run `uv run evaluate`; public challenges are hosted on Codabench and external challenge sites.
participation.submissionFormat: Agent trajectories ({run_id}.json) + evaluation report, or a challenge submission on the external competition site.
participation.computeDetails: Agents call LLMs via LiteLLM proxy / TokenRouter; no training compute required, inference API access needed.
participation.rounds: Scenario suites (mini / lite / all), public challenges (CODS 2025 completed, IJCAI 2026 live)
participation.verification: Offline evaluator (LLM-as-judge 6-criterion rubric plus static JSON scorers) run over saved trajectories.

venue.event: IJCAI 2026 Industrial Automation Challenge (co-located); CODS 2025 AssetOpsBench-Live

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/IBM/AssetOpsBench.git
cd AssetOpsBench
uv sync
cp .env.public .env
# run a scenario with an agent, then evaluate saved trajectories
uv run evaluate --leaderboard <leaderboard_dir>

competitions.name: AlpacaEval
competitions.tagline: Automatic LLM-as-judge benchmark measuring instruction-following win rate against a reference model.
competitions.description: AlpacaEval evaluates instruction-following chat models by having a strong LLM annotator (e.g. GPT-4-turbo) compare a model's outputs against a reference model's outputs on the 805-example AlpacaEval set, reporting win rate and length-controlled win rate. It is fast (<5 min) and cheap (<$10) and correlates 0.98 with ChatBot Arena. Maintained by the tatsu-lab (Stanford) team; anyone can submit a model via a pull request adding a model config, outputs, and a leaderboard entry.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repo, add a model config under src/alpaca_eval/models_configs/<model_name>, run `alpaca_eval evaluate_from_model --model_configs '<model_name>'`, then open a PR adding the config, outputs, and updated leaderboard entry.
participation.submissionFormat: Model config YAML, model_outputs.json, annotations.json, and updated leaderboard CSV under src/alpaca_eval/leaderboards/
participation.computeDetails: GPU needed only for local HuggingFace model decoding; annotation is done via API (e.g. OpenAI).
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; top-5 models can request verification by maintainers.
participation.cost: free (plus annotator API costs, <$10 per run)
participation.verification: Community submissions via PR; top-5 models can be verified by a core maintainer who re-decodes and re-evaluates.
requirements: OpenAI API key (or other annotator provider)

competitions.quickstart:
pip install alpaca-eval
export OPENAI_API_KEY=<your_api_key>
alpaca_eval --model_outputs 'example/outputs.json' --annotators_config 'weighted_alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo'

competitions.name: VBench
competitions.tagline: Benchmark and leaderboard for video generative models across quality, semantic, and faithfulness dimensions.
competitions.description: VBench is a comprehensive benchmark suite for video generative models, decomposing video generation quality into hierarchical evaluation dimensions with dedicated prompt suites and automatic evaluation methods. Models are scored per dimension, then aggregated into Quality, Semantic, and Total scores (VBench), I2V and Quality scores (VBench-I2V), or Creativity/Commonsense/Controllability/Human Fidelity/Physics scores (VBench-2.0). It is maintained by the Vchitect team and hosted on Hugging Face, with submissions accepted via evaluation result JSON files.

participation.howToSubmit: Run the evaluation scripts locally, pack the evaluation_results directory into a zip, optionally compute the final score with scripts/cal_final_score.py, then submit the JSON to the Hugging Face leaderboard space.
participation.submissionFormat: evaluation_results.zip containing per-dimension JSON results; optionally a computed total score JSON.
participation.computeDetails: Evaluation requires GPU (CUDA) for feature extractors such as DINO, RAFT, UMT, ViCLIP; VBench-2.0 recommends up to 8 GPUs for parallel dimension evaluation.
participation.eligibility: Open to all video generative model developers and researchers.
participation.verification: Automatic evaluation scripts and leaderboard submission review; results are reproducible via provided code.

competitions.quickstart:
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118
pip install vbench
vbench evaluate --videos_path $VIDEO_PATH --dimension $DIMENSION
cd evaluation_results && zip -r ../evaluation_results.zip .
python scripts/cal_final_score.py --zip_file evaluation_results.zip --model_name your_model_name

competitions.name: Chess Coding Challenge
competitions.tagline: Write a tiny C# chess bot under a 1024-token limit that wins games against other bots.
competitions.description: Participants implement a chess bot in a single MyBot.cs file using the provided C# framework, with code size capped at 1024 tokens and only a restricted set of namespaces allowed. Submissions were entered via a Google Form and then played in a large Swiss tournament followed by a knockout playoff to determine the best bot. The challenge is run by Sebastian Lague and drew 636 submitted bots; results are published in a separate results repository.

participation.howToSubmit: Fill out the Google Form submission page with your MyBot.cs entry; entries could be edited until submissions closed.
participation.submissionFormat: A single MyBot.cs file containing the MyBot struct and Think function, within the 1024-token bot brain capacity.
participation.computeDetails: Bots run locally for testing; tournament games are played by the organizers.
participation.rounds: Large Swiss tournament followed by a knockout tournament for top bots.
participation.eligibility: Open to individuals or groups of any size; maximum two entries per participant.
participation.verification: Organizers run submitted bots in the official tournament; illegal moves or timeouts lose the game.

problems.description: Create a C# chess bot within a 1024-token code limit that plays legal chess and wins games in the tournament.
problems.name: Tiny Chess Bot

competitions.name: MLE-bench
competitions.tagline: Agents solve 75 Kaggle ML engineering competitions; scored by percentage of medals won within a time budget.
competitions.description: MLE-bench evaluates AI agents on 75 Kaggle competitions, measuring the percentage of competitions where the agent's submission earns a medal (Any Medal %). Submissions are graded against held-out test splits using the repo's grading scripts, and results are reported as mean ± SEM over at least 3 seeds. It is maintained by OpenAI and is a standard benchmark for autonomous ML engineering agents.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to main adding grading reports under runs/<run-group>/ and register the run group in runs/run_group_experiments.csv with an experiment id; then report aggregated scores in the README leaderboard table.
participation.submissionFormat: Grading report JSON files per run group in runs/, plus a row in the README leaderboard table with mean ± SEM for Low/Lite, Medium, High, and All splits.
participation.computeDetails: Recommended: 36 vCPUs, 440GB RAM, one 24GB A10 GPU, 24-hour runtime per competition.
participation.rounds: Continuous leaderboard; submissions currently paused (as of 2026-04-24) while a new fairness process is developed.
participation.eligibility: Open to any team or individual; agents must not use test-set labels.
participation.verification: Grading reports reviewed by maintainers; rule violation and plagiarism detectors available; test-set feedback submissions flagged separately.

competitions.tagline: Rank LLMs by ELO from real-time Street Fighter III matches where models pick moves from text or screenshots.
competitions.description: LLM Colosseum pits language and multimodal models against each other in real-time Street Fighter III (3rd Strike) via the Diambra arcade environment. The benchmark is run by the OpenGenerativeAI team (phospho and Quivr) and tests speed, strategy, adaptability and resilience of LLMs in a fast, adversarial setting.

participation.eligibility: Open to anyone who opens a PR.
participation.verification: Maintainers run matches and update the ELO ranking; PR review by maintainers.
requirements: API keys for the model provider (or Ollama for local models)

competitions.name: Polymarket Paper Trader / Forecast Arena
competitions.tagline: Forecast real Polymarket questions before they resolve and get scored by Brier score against the crowd.
competitions.description: A zero-risk paper-trading gym and benchmark for AI agents on live Polymarket prediction markets. The Forecast Arena is a daily public leaderboard where AI models and naive baselines each publish one YES probability per soon-resolving binary market before it resolves, then are scored by real outcomes (Brier score, ECE, alpha vs crowd). A separate paper-trading leaderboard ranks agents by ROI% on a fixed $10,000 paper balance. Run by agent-next; the arena data is append-only on an arena-data branch.

participation.howToSubmit: Forecast Arena: add an entrant block to benchmark/arena.yaml (id, label, kind, model, disclosure metadata) and open a PR; the daily CI workflow runs predict/resolve/build. Paper-trading leaderboard: generate a leaderboard_entry via the MCP tool or `pm-trader leaderboard` and open an issue with the JSON.
participation.submissionFormat: arena.yaml entrant block (id, label, kind ai|baseline, model litellm id, api_base/api_key_env, web_access, cutoff); or a GitHub issue titled `[SUBMIT] {agent_name} — ROI: {roi}%` with the leaderboard_entry JSON body.
participation.computeDetails: Forecasting is a single-shot LLM call per market; no GPU or local compute required.
participation.rounds: Daily runs; markets selected each day ending in 0-14 days.
participation.eligibility: Open to any model provider or agent author; AI entrants and deterministic baselines.
participation.verification: Append-only JSONL on the arena-data branch; CI workflow runs predict/resolve/build; leaderboard rows expose model id and forecast timestamps as an audit trail.
requirements: litellm-compatible model endpoint or API key

competitions.quickstart:
pip install -e "benchmark[dev]"
polymarket-benchmark arena predict --data /tmp/arena-data
polymarket-benchmark arena resolve --data /tmp/arena-data
polymarket-benchmark arena build --data /tmp/arena-data --out site/

problems.description: AI agents trade Polymarket with a fixed $10,000 paper balance against live order books; ranked by ROI% with Sharpe ratio as tiebreaker. Minimum 10 trades to qualify.

competitions.name: Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark (SKAB)
competitions.tagline: Benchmark for outlier and changepoint detection on multivariate time series from a water pump testbed.
competitions.description: SKAB provides a benchmark of 34 datasets with collective anomalies from a physical industrial testbed. It evaluates algorithms on two tasks: outlier detection (point anomalies) and changepoint detection (collective anomalies). The leaderboard ranks algorithms by F1 for outlier detection and NAB score for changepoint detection. Submissions are made via Kaggle, where the benchmark is hosted.

participation.howToSubmit: Submit your algorithm and results on the Kaggle competition page.
participation.submissionFormat: Algorithm predictions and evaluation on Kaggle.
participation.computeDetails: The benchmark datasets are relatively small; no GPU is required.
participation.verification: Submissions are evaluated on Kaggle using the provided evaluation metrics.

competitions.quickstart:

competitions.tagline: Decide whether one magma law implies another and submit a machine-verifiable Lean 4 certificate.
competitions.description: Given two equational laws E1 and E2 over magmas, contestants must decide whether E1 implies E2 and supply a Lean 4 certificate: a proof for true implications or a magma witness (finite or infinite) for false ones. A deterministic Lean judge verifies each answer with no partial credit and no LLM-as-judge, mapping it to accepted/unparsed/malformed/incomplete_proof/incorrect. The submission is a single solver.py (<=500 KB) running under organizer-controlled LLM budgets. Run by SAIR (Sovereign AI Research) as Stage 2 of the Mathematics Distillation Challenge; the underlying corpus comes from Terence Tao's Equational Theories Project.

competitions.description: A collection of small, self-contained benchmark problems from the Sutro Group's energy-efficient learning research. competitions.name: LeanEval
competitions.tagline: Prove open formalization problems in Lean 4; models and submitters are ranked by problems solved.
competitions.description: LeanEval is the Lean FRO's comparator-based benchmark for formal mathematics. Trusted theorem statements live in leanprover/lean-eval; a problem counts as solved when the comparator accepts a submitted proof. Results are sticky per (user, model, problem) and published at lean-lang.org/eval. 304 visible problems, 75 models, 60 submitters, 39 active problems still unsolved.

participation.howToSubmit: Prove a problem's theorem in your own GitHub repository and submit the ref at lean-lang.org/eval/submit; the comparator verifies the proof and the result is appended to results/<login>.json in leanprover/lean-eval-submissions.
participation.submissionFormat: GitHub repo + ref containing the completed Lean proof, plus the declared model label used to produce it.
participation.computeDetails: Scoring is a comparator check of the proof; whatever compute the prover needs is on the submitter's side.
participation.eligibility: Open to everyone. Successes are sticky: an accepted (user, model, problem) tuple is never removed.
participation.verification: Comparator acceptance in CI, replay by maintainers, public audit log per user.

participation.verification: CI validates the JSON, verifies GitHub run URLs via the GitHub API, checks artifact attestations for github_actions rows, and runs a leaderboard audit (accept/review/reject). Maintainer reruns are stored separately.

competitions.tagline: Train an ONNX policy that walks a Unitree G1 through a 51 m parkour course under randomized friction and wind.
competitions.description: Miners submit an ONNX policy (<=15 MB, architecture free) that drives a 12-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid through a 51.1 m linear parkour course: on-ramp, drop, stairs, a 1 m leap, hurdle, step-up, duck-under, balance beam, slick patch and stairway down. Each round evaluates 24 instances of up to 3000 control steps with friction and wind drawn from an unpublished per-round seed, so open-loop trajectory replay is worthless. Scoring is progress-based: completions score in (1.0, 2.0] with a speed bonus, non-completions score their fraction of course covered, and raw_score is the mean over 24 instances. Run by Macrocosm (Apex competition, Bittensor Subnet 1); the reference Unitree stock walker reaches only 21% of the course.

participation.howToSubmit: Submit an ONNX policy graph through the Apex platform (Bittensor Subnet 1); the referee runs it in the player sandbox against 24 randomized instances.
participation.submissionFormat: ONNX graph, <= 15 MB, float32, interface obs[104] + state_in[256] -> action[12] + state_out[256]; architecture free (recurrent nets, ensembles, transformers over a history window).
participation.computeDetails: Referee runs under --cpus 1 --memory 1.5g; inference runs once per control step up to 72,000 times per evaluation, with a 900 s referee timeout. Training a policy is the miner's own responsibility.
participation.rounds: Rounds with per-round seeds; conditions (friction, wind) drawn per round and not published while the round is open.
participation.verification: Referee container runs the policy in a player sandbox; physics_glitch/invalid/player errors score 0.0; history and API log artifacts are collected per submission.

competitions.name: SqueezeBench
competitions.tagline: Prove Lean-verified lower and upper bounds that squeeze intractable extremal-combinatorics functions f(n).
competitions.description: SqueezeBench keeps, for each extremal-combinatorics problem, the best Lean-proved lower bound and the best Lean-proved upper bound on a function f : ℕ → ℕ (Ramsey, Schur, cap sets, Golomb rulers, ex(n; C₄), etc.). A submission is a new record version: a Lean function plus machine-checked proofs of valid, improves and strict, judged by Comparator against a frozen statement and checked by two independent kernels (Lean and nanoda). It is run by the SqueezeBench team (Pablo Manrique, Hai Xia, Stefan Szeider) and doubles as a saturation-resilient evaluation of AI mathematical capability.

participation.howToSubmit: Run `lake exe squeeze new <Problem> <lower|upper>` to lay out the next version, write Def.lean and Proof.lean, fill in REPORT.md and metadata.toml, run `lake exe squeeze verify <record-dir> --base upstream/main`, then open a PR that adds your record directory and nothing else.
participation.submissionFormat: One new record directory under SqueezeBench/Problems/<Problem>/Records/<Lower|Upper>/V<k>/ containing Def.lean, Proof.lean, REPORT.md and metadata.toml.
participation.computeDetails: Proof checking is CPU-only; `squeeze verify`'s fuel check alone peaks near 7 GB, and the Comparator runs in its own 16 GB unit.
participation.verification: Comparator judges against a statement frozen for that version; every proof is checked by Lean's kernel and by nanoda (Rust re-implementation). No sorry, no new axioms, no native_decide.

organizer.name: SqueezeBench team (Pablo Manrique, Hai Xia, Stefan Szeider)

competitions.name: SWE-bench Pro Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Score coding agents on 731 real-world software engineering tasks by the fraction of instances whose test suites pass.
competitions.description: A leaderboard for evaluating coding agents on SWE-bench Pro, a dataset of 731 real-world software engineering tasks. A green agent sends each instance (problem statement + Docker image) to a submitted coding agent, collects the returned patch, and runs the project's test suite in Docker; an instance passes only if all FAIL_TO_PASS tests pass and all PASS_TO_PASS tests still pass. Final score is accuracy = passed / total. Run by the RDI Foundation via the AgentBeats platform.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repo, set your agent's Agentbeats ID in scenario.json5 (metadata.agentbeats_ids.coding_agent), add provider API keys as repo secrets, then open/update a PR to main or trigger the 'Run Scenario' workflow from the Actions tab; follow the PR link in the workflow summary to submit results. Alternatively submit through agentbeats.dev via OIDC quick-submit.
participation.submissionFormat: scenario.json5 configuration plus a results JSON produced by the green agent (per-instance pass/fail and accuracy); quick-submit via agentbeats.dev UI.
participation.computeDetails: Evaluation runs each SWE-bench Pro instance in a Docker container; agent inference depends on the chosen model provider. Local runs can be sharded via assessment_config.num_instances / num_shards.
participation.verification: Automated: green agent runs FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests in Docker; results committed as results/<uuid>.json via CI workflows.
